title: Before He Called Her Wife, He Chose to Protect Her
paragraphs:
Before He Called Her Wife, He Chose to Protect Her
The Forgotten Love Story That Reveals Why Godly Men Guard a Woman's Dignity Before They Ever Hold Her Hand
Have you ever wondered why one of the greatest love stories ever recorded in Scripture contains almost no romance?
Perhaps that is exactly why it has survived thousands of years.
Because the Book of Ruth was never meant to teach us how to fall in love.
It was written to show us how redeemed people love after they have first learned to fear God.
In a world where relationships often begin with taking, Boaz began with giving.
In a culture obsessed with possession, Boaz chose protection.
Long before Ruth ever became his bride...
She first became someone he refused to let be harmed.
Because this story has never really been about romance.
It has always been about redemption.
And if you look closely enough...
You'll discover the Gospel hidden inside every chapter.
Her future appears buried beneath grief.
Beside her stands Ruth, a Moabite widow.

Moab originated from the incestuous union between Lot and his eldest daughter (Genesis 19:30–38). Later, Moab repeatedly opposed Israel and seduced them into idolatry (Numbers 25:1–3). Deuteronomy 23:3 declared:
"No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD..."
At first glance, Ruth seems like the least likely person to become part of God's covenant story.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reminds us that God's grace reaches where human prejudice cannot.
The Hebrew word for grace is חֵן (ḥēn).
It means favour that cannot be earned.
Beauty that comes from God's delight rather than human merit.
Long before Ruth found acceptance among God's people...
God's grace had already begun pursuing her.
Every believer has stood where Ruth once stood.
That is why Ruth's story quietly whispers the Gospel centuries before Jesus was born.
When Ruth went to glean behind the harvesters according to God's provision for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10), she unknowingly entered the field belonging to Boaz.
But the Hebrew tells the story with beautiful irony.
God had already arranged every step.
There are no accidents in the providence of God.
Only appointments we fail to recognize until later.
He had heard of her loyalty.
"Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised."
The world trains us to admire faces.
God trains us to discern hearts.
Then comes one of the most remarkable moments in all of Scripture.
"I have ordered the young men not to touch you." (Ruth 2:8–9)
Boaz was not merely being polite.
He used his authority to protect a vulnerable woman from harassment, exploitation, abuse, and humiliation.
He had absolutely no obligation to do this.
She belonged to no one who could defend her.
Yet Boaz chose to become her protector before he ever became her husband.
"What can I get from this relationship?"
"How can I make sure she is safe?"
There is an ocean of difference.
"Even pull out some stalks for her from the bundles and leave them for her to gather. Don't rebuke her." (Ruth 2:16)
Kindness that expected nothing in return.
The Hebrew concept behind Boaz's actions is חֶסֶד (ḥesed).
No single English word fully captures it.
Throughout the Old Testament, ḥesed describes God's covenant love toward His people.
This is why many theologians describe Boaz as a type—a foreshadowing—of Christ.
But because his actions point beyond himself.
Jesus came to redeem the vulnerable.
Jesus paid a price others could never afford.
Under Israel's law (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 25), a close relative could redeem family property, preserve the family line, and rescue relatives from irreversible loss.
Jesus would become our greater Go'el.
The New Testament uses the Greek word ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis).
Release through the payment of a ransom.
Boaz redeemed Ruth with silver and legal authority.
Jesus redeemed sinners with His own blood.
Christ restores everyone who comes to Him in faith.
This is why the Book of Ruth belongs in the larger story of redemption.
Its final chapter quietly reveals something astonishing.
Boaz and Ruth become the great-grandparents of King David (Ruth 4:17–22).
Matthew's Gospel then includes Ruth among the women in Jesus Christ's genealogy (Matthew 1:5).
Becomes part of the family line through which the Messiah enters the world.
Only God writes stories like that.
The scandal of Ruth's past did not disqualify her from God's future.
That has always been the theme of Scripture.
Because the Bible is ultimately not a collection of flawless heroes.
It is the story of a flawless Saviour.
Perhaps you have been living as though your failures define you.
Maybe shame has convinced you that God can forgive others but not you.
Your past may explain where you have been.
It does not determine where Christ can take you.
Jesus still writes better endings than we deserve.
Not that good people become acceptable.
But that guilty people are justified by grace through faith in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 3:23–24).
Boaz protected Ruth before he married her because true covenant love seeks another person's good before seeking personal gain.
"But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
He loved us before we loved Him.
He pursued us before we sought Him.
He redeemed us before we could repay Him.
He covered our shame before clothing us with His righteousness.
The Greek word ἀγάπη (agapē) describes this self-giving, sacrificial love—love that seeks the highest good of another regardless of personal cost. That is the love ultimately displayed at the cross.
If you are a man, ask yourself:
Do the women around you feel safer because you are present?
Do your words honour their dignity?
Does your strength protect rather than pressure?
If you are a woman, remember Ruth.
Your worth was never determined by your past, your status, your nationality, or the opinions of others.
Your identity is found in the God who delights to redeem.
And if you belong to Christ, remember this:
You were once the outsider in the field.
He gave you a new name.
He welcomed you into His family.
That is why our ministry exists.
Not simply to create Christian resources.
But to point hearts to Jesus Christ—the only Redeemer who never fails.

If this article strengthened your faith, would you prayerfully consider helping us proclaim this Gospel even further? If your desire is to glorify God by helping His Word spread, your support becomes part of that work.
While these resources are never a substitute for Scripture, they are designed to encourage daily discipleship, spark gospel conversations, and keep Christ at the centre of everyday life.
Your testimony may encourage someone who is wondering whether redemption is still possible for them.
You never know how God may use a simple act of faithfulness to begin rewriting another life through the Gospel.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God changes your circumstances...
It's that He changes your identity.
